json.title: JSON
json.tagline: The lingua franca of the web: data as plain text.

meta.title: What is JSON — history, structure, conversions
meta.description: JSON explained: origins at Netscape, why it beat XML, syntax rules, common pitfalls — and free browser-based JSON ↔ YAML/TOML/CSV/XML conversion.

json.history:
JSON was formalized by Douglas Crockford around 2001, building on JavaScript object literal syntax from the mid-90s. The joke in the name is real: 'JavaScript Object Notation' was never meant to be a standard — Crockford famously said he 'discovered' it rather than invented it.
The spec (RFC 8259) fits on a few pages, which is exactly why it won. By 2005–2010 JSON displaced XML in web APIs almost everywhere: it was lighter to parse, easier to read, and every language could map its types natively.
Today it's the default interchange format for APIs, config files (package.json, tsconfig.json), logs, and databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB).
json.how:
A JSON document has exactly six value types: object («…»), array («[…]»), string, number, boolean, and null. Strings are double-quoted; numbers are decimal (no hex, no NaN); trailing commas are forbidden.
Everything else you see in 'JSON-like' files — comments, single quotes, unquoted keys — is a dialect (JSON5, HJSON), not JSON itself. That strictness is a feature: a parser can be tiny and fast.
Whitespace between tokens is insignificant, so pretty-printing and minifying are lossless operations — that's what our JSON pretty / minify / sort-keys converters do.

yaml.title: YAML
yaml.tagline: Config format that looks like prose.

meta.title: What is YAML — history, indentation, pitfalls
meta.description: YAML explained: from 'Yet Another Markup Language' to Kubernetes configs, indentation rules, the Norway problem — and free YAML ↔ JSON conversion in your browser.

yaml.history:
YAML appeared in 2001, created by Clark Evans, Ingy döt Net and Oren Ben-Kiki. The original backronym was 'Yet Another Markup Language'; later the authors re-branded it 'YAML Ain't Markup Language' to emphasize it describes data, not documents.
Its killer feature was human-friendliness: no braces, minimal quoting, indentation instead of punctuation. That made it the config language of DevOps era — Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Ansible all speak YAML.
yaml.how:
Structure comes from indentation: two spaces per level is convention (tabs are forbidden). Key-value pairs are `key: value`; lists use dashes; nested structures just indent further.
Scalars are auto-typed: `true`, `42`, `3.14` become bool/number — this is the source of the famous 'Norway problem', where country code `no` silently becomes boolean false. Quoting a value forces string interpretation.
UWC implements the practical subset of YAML — mappings, sequences, scalars, quoted strings — which covers virtually all real-world configs.

toml.title: TOML
toml.tagline: Obvious config format for humans and parsers alike.

meta.title: What is TOML — history, tables, when to use it
meta.description: TOML explained: Tom Preston-Werner's answer to YAML, tables and arrays of tables, why Rust and Python adopted it — and free TOML ↔ JSON conversion.

toml.history:
TOML ('Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language') was created in 2013 by Tom Preston-Werner, co-founder of GitHub, out of frustration with YAML's edge cases and INI's flatness.
It found its home in package ecosystems: Cargo (Rust) made it mandatory, Python's pyproject.toml followed, and now it's the de-facto standard for project metadata.
toml.how:
TOML reads like INI with a type system: `key = value` lines, `[table]` headers for nesting, `[[array-of-tables]]` for lists of records. Values are strictly typed — strings, integers, floats, booleans, dates, arrays, inline tables.
Unlike YAML there's exactly one way to write each structure, so parsers agree with each other — no Norway problem, no surprise booleans.
UWC parses the full core spec: tables, dotted keys, inline tables, arrays of tables, dates.

csv.title: CSV
csv.tagline: Fifty years old and still everywhere: spreadsheets as text.

meta.title: What is CSV — history, dialects, escaping rules
meta.description: CSV explained: from IBM Fortran programs to Excel, delimiter and quoting dialects, why 'the CSV from hell' exists — and free CSV ↔ JSON/TSV conversion.

csv.history:
Comma-separated values predate the PC: IBM's Fortran routines used them in 1972, and by the early 80s the format was the de-facto way to move spreadsheet data. Ironically, CSV was only standardized in RFC 4180 (2005) — decades after everyone started using it their own way.
That late standardization is why 'CSV dialect hell' exists: semicolons in Europe, tabs in TSV, quoting rules that vary by tool.
csv.how:
A CSV row is a line, fields are separated by a delimiter (comma, semicolon, tab). If a field contains the delimiter, quotes or newlines, it's wrapped in double quotes; embedded quotes are doubled (`""`).
There's no type system — everything is text until you decide otherwise. UWC's parser handles quoted fields, escaped quotes and both LF/CRLF line endings, and its coerceScalar policy mirrors spreadsheet behavior: unquoted scalars become numbers or booleans, quoted stay strings.

xml.title: XML
xml.tagline: The verbose giant that still runs the world's paperwork.

meta.title: What is XML — history, structure, where it survives
meta.description: XML explained: SGML roots, SOAP era, namespaces and attributes, where XML is still required — and free XML ↔ JSON conversion in the browser.

xml.history:
XML was born in 1996–1998 at the W3C as a simplified subset of SGML, the document format behind HTML. The late 90s bet everything on it: SOAP web services, Office file formats, RSS feeds, Android layouts.
JSON took the web-API crown in the 2010s, but XML never left: office documents (DOCX/XLSX are zipped XML), SVG, RSS/Atom, Maven, Android UI, and half of enterprise B2B still run on it.
xml.how:
XML is a tree of tagged elements: 〈item attr="value"〉content〈/item〉. Elements nest; attributes carry metadata; text lives between tags. Namespaces (xmlns) prevent collisions between vocabularies.
The eternal conversion question is what to do with attributes vs child elements — UWC maps attributes under a reserved key and keeps the round-trip lossless enough for real-world documents.

base64.title: Base64
base64.tagline: Binary data wearing a text costume.

meta.title: What is Base64 — history, padding, URL-safe variants
meta.description: Base64 explained: email attachments origin, how 6-bit groups work, = padding, URL-safe alphabet — and instant Base64 encode/decode in your browser.

base64.history: Base64 comes from PEM (1987) and early email: SMTP could only carry 7-bit ASCII, so binary attachments needed a text costume. MIME standardized it in 1992–1996, and the web reused it for Data URIs, JWT tokens and CSS-embedded images.
base64.how:
Take 3 bytes (24 bits), split into four 6-bit groups, map each 0–63 value onto the alphabet A–Z a–z 0–9 + /. When the input isn't divisible by 3, `=` padding fills the tail — that's why Base64 strings often end with one or two equals signs.
Size grows ~33% (4 characters per 3 bytes). The URL-safe variant swaps `+/` for `-_` so tokens survive in URLs without percent-encoding.
Decoding is pure math — UWC does it instantly, UTF-8 safe, entirely offline.

png.title: PNG
png.tagline: Lossless pixels, born out of a licensing dispute.

meta.title: PNG format — history, compression, transparency
meta.description: PNG explained: the 1995 Usenet sprint against Unisys GIF patents, DEFLATE filtering, alpha transparency — and free PNG ↔ WebP/JPEG/AVIF conversion.

png.history:
PNG was born in January 1995, after Unisys announced it would charge royalties for LZW compression used in GIF. Within weeks, developers on Usenet drafted a patent-free replacement; version 1.0 shipped in 1996 and became an ISO standard in 2003.
The name is an explicit recursive joke: 'PNG's Not GIF'.
png.how:
A PNG file is a sequence of chunks: IHDR (dimensions, bit depth), IDAT (compressed pixel data), IEND. Pixels pass through per-row filters (sub/up/average/paeth) that make neighbors predictable, then DEFLATE compresses the result — the same algorithm as ZIP.
It supports full 8-bit alpha transparency and lossless storage, which makes it ideal for screenshots, UI and graphics with sharp edges. For photos, JPEG/WebP/AVIF are far smaller.
UWC converts PNG to modern formats via canvas in your browser, and heavy targets (AVIF, TIFF, ICO) through its server — either way, images aren't stored.

jpeg.title: JPEG
jpeg.tagline: Thirty years of photos in 8×8 blocks.

meta.title: JPEG format — history, DCT compression, artifacts
meta.description: JPEG explained: the Joint Photographic Experts Group, discrete cosine transform, quality settings, why JPEG artifacts appear — and free JPEG ↔ WebP/PNG/AVIF conversion.

jpeg.history: JPEG was published in 1992 by the Joint Photographic Experts Group — an ISO/IEC committee that spent years balancing quality against the storage realities of the early 90s (a CD held ~650 MB). It became the universal photo format and stayed there for three decades.
jpeg.how:
The image is cut into 8×8 pixel blocks. Each block goes through the discrete cosine transform (DCT), turning pixels into frequency coefficients; high frequencies (fine detail) get quantized away — that's where the size savings and the familiar 'blocky' artifacts come from.
Chroma subsampling halves color resolution because eyes are worse at color than brightness. Quality setting (roughly 60–85) is the sweet spot for photos.
JPEG has no alpha channel — transparency requires PNG/WebP/AVIF. UWC flattens transparency to white when producing JPEG, exactly like browsers do.

webp.title: WebP
webp.tagline: Google's bet that made the web 30% lighter.

meta.title: WebP format — history, VP8 internals, browser support
meta.description: WebP explained: On2 VP8 heritage, 2010 launch, Safari's late arrival, lossy and lossless modes — and free WebP ↔ PNG/JPEG/AVIF conversion.

webp.history:
Google announced WebP in 2010, deriving the codec from the VP8 video encoder it had acquired with On2 Technologies. The pitch: same visual quality as JPEG at 25–35% less size.
Adoption was slow — Firefox waited until 2020, Safari until 2020 (iOS 14). Today it's universally supported and powers a large share of web images.
webp.how:
WebP has two personalities: lossy mode uses VP8 intra-frame coding (predictive blocks + DCT residuals), while lossless mode uses a completely different transform designed for exact reproduction.
It also supports alpha transparency even in lossy mode — something JPEG never managed — plus animation.
For screenshots and UI, WebP-lossless usually beats PNG by 20–30%; for photos, WebP-lossy beats JPEG similarly.

gif.title: GIF
gif.tagline: 1987 called: it wants to keep animating.

meta.title: GIF format — history, LZW compression, animation
meta.description: GIF explained: CompuServe origins, the Unisys patent saga, 256-color palette, frame-based animation — and free GIF ↔ PNG/WebP conversion.

gif.history:
Steve Wilhite at CompuServe created GIF in 1987 to compress color images over dial-up modems. Version 89a added animation and transparency — features that accidentally made GIF the meme format of the internet.
The Unisys LZW patent controversy in 1994–2004 directly spawned PNG. And yes: the author said it's pronounced 'jif', the internet disagreed, the debate continues.
gif.how:
GIF stores up to 256 colors per frame using LZW compression — great for logos and pixel art, terrible for photos (dithering banding). Animation is just multiple frames with per-frame timing and optional transparency.
Each frame is typically stored as a delta against the previous one, which is why optimized GIFs are much smaller than naive exports.
Modern alternatives: WebP/AVIF animations are 10–50× smaller at similar quality. UWC converts static GIF frames to PNG/WebP in the browser.

svg.title: SVG

meta.title: SVG format — history, vector graphics, security notes
meta.description: SVG explained: W3C XML vector format, shapes and paths, why it scales infinitely, sanitization concerns — and free SVG ↔ PNG conversion.

svg.history: The W3C released SVG 1.0 in 2001 after years of competing vector proposals. It languished for a decade — IE didn't support it until 2011 — then exploded once responsive design made resolution independence essential. Today it's the default for icons, logos and charts.
svg.how:
SVG is XML describing geometry: 〈circle〉, 〈rect〉, 〈path d="M…"〉 commands, filled and stroked with colors/gradients. Because shapes are formulas, not pixels, they render crisp at any zoom level and weigh kilobytes.
Security note: SVG can embed scripts, which is why UWC renders it through 〈img〉/canvas rather than injecting raw markup into the page — and why server-side rasterization happens in an isolated pipeline.

heic.title: HEIC
heic.tagline: Apple's efficient photo format your computer loves to hate.

meta.title: HEIC format — history, HEVC container, converting iPhone photos
meta.description: HEIC explained: High Efficiency Image Container, HEVC/H.265 internals, why iPhones default to it, compatibility pain — and free HEIC → PNG/JPEG/WebP conversion.

heic.history: HEIC is the still-image sibling of HEVC (H.265) video, standardized in 2015 by MPEG. Apple made it the default iPhone camera format in iOS 11 (2017) — halving photo sizes overnight and creating a decade-long support headache for everyone else.
heic.how:
A HEIC file is an ISOBMFF container (same family as MP4) holding HEVC-coded image data, possibly multiple images (Live Photos, bursts) and depth maps.
Compression is dramatically better than JPEG — similar quality at roughly half the size — but decoding requires HEVC patents, which is why OS support lagged: Windows needs extensions, older software simply fails.
UWC decodes HEIC via libheif WASM and hands pixels to sharp — your iPhone photos become PNG/JPEG/WebP without installing anything.

ico.title: ICO
ico.tagline: The little file that lives in your browser tab.

meta.title: ICO format — history, multi-resolution containers, favicon
meta.description: ICO explained: Windows 1.0 heritage, multi-size containers, BMP and PNG frames, favicon usage — and free ICO ↔ PNG conversion.

ico.history:
ICO dates back to Windows 1.0 (1985) as the format for interface icons. Its defining trick — packing several resolutions in one file — appeared early, because the same icon had to look right at 16×16 in a title bar and 32×32 on a desktop.
On the web it survives as favicon.ico, the one file every site still ships by convention.
ico.how:
An ICO is a tiny container: a header, a directory of image entries, then the images themselves — historically BMP-with-alpha (DIB), nowadays often embedded PNG for larger sizes.
That's why ICO handling is really container handling: pick the best frame, decode it, done. UWC's parser selects the largest/most colorful frame and writes Vista+ PNG-format icons back.

mp3.title: MP3
mp3.tagline: The format that put a thousand songs in your pocket.

meta.title: MP3 format — history, psychoacoustics, MP3 vs AAC/Opus
meta.description: MP3 explained: Fraunhofer research, perceptual audio coding, the patent expiry of 2017, why it survived — and free MP3 ↔ WAV/FLAC/OGG conversion in the browser.

mp3.history:
MP3 grew out of Fraunhofer's EUREKA research in the late 80s and was finalized as MPEG-1 Audio Layer III in 1993. It rode Napster and portable players to total cultural dominance in 1999–2005.
All patents expired in April 2017 — the format is now completely free, which is why it refuses to die despite technically superior successors.
mp3.how:
MP3 is lossy: it chops audio into frequency bands and discards what psychoacoustic models say you can't hear — quiet sounds next to loud ones, frequencies above ~16 kHz at typical bitrates. At 128–192 kbps VBR most listeners can't tell it from CD audio.
Decoding is lossless in the sense that every player produces identical PCM; encoding always loses information. Converting MP3 → FLAC doesn't restore quality, it just stops further loss.
UWC decodes MP3 with the browser's own Web Audio engine and re-encodes to WAV/FLAC/OGG/Opus locally — no ffmpeg, no uploads.

wav.title: WAV

meta.title: WAV format — history, RIFF container, PCM audio
meta.description: WAV explained: IBM/Microsoft RIFF container from 1991, PCM samples, bit depth and sample rate, why editors love it — and free WAV ↔ MP3/FLAC/Opus conversion.

wav.history: WAV arrived in 1991 as part of RIFF, the IBM/Microsoft resource-interchange framework for Windows 3.1 multimedia. Thirty-plus years later it remains the lingua franca of audio editing precisely because it does almost nothing.
wav.how:
A WAV is a RIFF container wrapping a `fmt ` chunk (sample rate, bit depth, channel count) and a `data` chunk of raw PCM samples — amplitude measurements taken tens of thousands of times per second.
CD quality is 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo ≈ 10 MB per minute. No compression means no artifacts, no decode latency, and trivial seeking — hence its role as the 'working' format in studios and pipelines.
UWC treats WAV as the hub of its audio pipeline: decoded PCM goes in, any target format comes out.

flac.title: FLAC
flac.tagline: Lossless compression for people who check spectrograms.

meta.title: FLAC format — history, linear prediction, lossless proof
meta.description: FLAC explained: Josh Coalson's 2001 codec, Xiph.Org stewardship, linear prediction + Rice coding, bit-perfect guarantee — and free FLAC ↔ WAV/MP3 conversion.

flac.history: Josh Coalson started FLAC in 2000; Xiph.Org adopted it in 2003. While MP3/Ogg Vorbis chased smallness, FLAC answered a different question: can we compress audio without losing a single bit? The answer, at ~50–60% of original size, made it the archive format for musicians, archivists and audiophiles.
flac.how:
FLAC exploits redundancy: neighboring samples correlate, so a linear predictor estimates the next sample and only the (small) residual gets entropy-coded with Rice coding. Decoding reproduces the original PCM bit-for-bit — verifiable via embedded MD5.
Being lossless and patent-free, it's the natural 'master copy' format: convert FLAC to anything, keep the original forever.
UWC decodes FLAC through Web Audio and encodes it back via {'@'}audio/encode — entirely in your browser.

ogg.title: OGG
ogg.tagline: The open-source answer to proprietary audio.

meta.title: Ogg Vorbis format — history, open-source codec, quality
meta.description: Ogg Vorbis explained: Xiph.Org's patent-free codec, better quality than MP3 at same bitrate, container vs codec confusion — and free OGG ↔ MP3/WAV conversion.

ogg.history:
Xiph.Org began Vorbis in 1998 explicitly as a patent-free alternative after it became clear MP3 wasn't free. Version 1.0 shipped in 2002. The name honors Terry Pratchett's Discworld character; 'Ogg' is technically the container, Vorbis the codec — but everyone says 'OGG'.
It became the darling of game developers (cheap licensing) and streaming services, and YouTube quietly serves Opus/Vorbis to capable clients.
ogg.how:
Vorbis is a transform codec like MP3 but with a more modern psychoacoustic model — at 128 kbps it generally matches MP3 at 160–192. The Ogg container pages packets with granule positions enabling precise seeking.
Common confusion: .ogg might contain Vorbis audio or Opus or even video (Theora) — sniffing the codec inside matters, which is exactly what magic-byte detection does.
UWC decodes OGG/Vorbis via Web Audio and re-encodes wherever you need.

zip.title: ZIP
zip.tagline: The archive that ate the world, one PK header at a time.

meta.title: ZIP format — history, DEFLATE, central directory
meta.description: ZIP explained: Phil Katz's 1989 format, PKWARE vs SEA lawsuit, central directory structure, zip bombs — and free ZIP extraction right in your browser.

zip.history: Phil Katz created ZIP in 1989 after a lawsuit with SEA (makers of ARC) — he wrote PKZIP from scratch in jail-released time, and the format's header magic `PK` are his initials. Katz's story ended tragically, but his format became the universal archive: DOS, Windows, Java JAR, Office DOCX, Android APK — all ZIP containers underneath.
zip.how:
A ZIP is a list of local file entries (name + compressed bytes) followed by a central directory at the end — that's why tools can list contents without reading the whole file, and why a truncated ZIP can sometimes be repaired.
Most entries use DEFLATE (the same algorithm as gzip). Entries are independent, so extraction can be lazy and parallel.
Danger notes: zip bombs (tiny archive, petabytes unpacked) and path traversal (`../../etc/passwd` names) are real attack vectors — any extractor must cap totals and sanitize paths. UWC unpacks in your browser with fflate, nothing touches a server.

tar.title: TAR
tar.tagline: Tape archive from 1979 that Linux can't live without.

meta.title: TAR format — history, 512-byte blocks, ustar headers
meta.description: TAR explained: Unix tape archives, ustar headers and 512-byte blocks, why tar.gz exists, path traversal risks — and TAR extraction in your browser.

tar.history:
TAR ('tape archive') appeared in Version 7 Unix (1979) for sequential backup to magnetic tape — hence fixed 512-byte blocks, which tape drives loved. POSIX standardized the ustar variant in 1988.
Unix philosophy kept TAR dumb: it concatenates files and metadata but doesn't compress. Compression came from outside — compress, later gzip, bzip2, xz — giving the world .tar.gz.
tar.how:
Each entry is a 512-byte header (name, mode, size in octal ASCII, checksum) followed by data padded to 512-byte multiples; two zero blocks end the archive. The ustar extension adds a prefix field for long paths.
No compression, no central directory — just a stream. That simplicity is why a correct parser is ~70 lines and why tar is the wrapper of choice for package formats (deb, RPM payloads).
Path traversal (`../` in names) is the classic TAR vulnerability — extractors must normalize paths. UWC parses TAR in your browser and shows entries before you download anything.

gzip.title: GZIP
gzip.tagline: DEFLATE with a header — the web's favorite compression.

meta.title: GZIP format — history, DEFLATE algorithm, HTTP compression
meta.description: GZIP explained: Jean-loup Gailly and Mark Adler, RFC 1952, DEFLATE internals, Content-Encoding on the web — and GZIP decompression in your browser.

gzip.history: Gzip was written in 1992 by Jean-loup Gailly and Mark Adler as a free replacement for the patented compress utility. Its payload algorithm, DEFLATE (RFC 1951), combined LZ77 matching with Huffman coding — and became arguably the most deployed compression algorithm in history: HTTP responses, PNG images, ZIP entries, git objects.
gzip.how:
The container is simple: a 10-byte header (magic `1f 8b`, flags, mtime), optionally a filename, then a raw DEFLATE stream, then CRC32 + length checks.
DEFLATE finds repeated byte sequences (LZ77 back-references) and Huffman-codes the result — repeated data costs almost nothing, random data barely shrinks.
On the web, `Content-Encoding: gzip` compresses HTML/CSS/JS by 70–80%. A .gz file holds exactly one stream — that's why tar.gz bundles exist: tar provides the many-files structure, gzip squeezes it.

qr.title: QR codes
qr.tagline: Denso Wave's masterpiece that survived its own patents.

meta.title: QR codes — history, error correction, versions
meta.description: QR codes explained: Denso Wave 1994, Reed-Solomon error correction, mask patterns, versions 1–40 — and free QR generation and scanning in your browser.

qr.history:
Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave invented the QR code in 1994 to track car parts on Toyota assembly lines — the 2D layout let workers scan codes at speed from any angle. Denso declined to exercise its patents, which is why QR conquered the planet instead of dying in a factory.
The pandemic turned it into everyday infrastructure: menus, tickets, payments.
qr.how:
A QR code is a grid of modules (21×21 for version 1 up to 177×177 for version 40) containing data encoded in bits, plus fixed function patterns: finder squares in corners, timing strips, format info.
The magic ingredient is Reed-Solomon error correction — up to 30% of the code can be damaged or covered (that's why logos-in-QR work) and it still scans. Mask patterns are applied to avoid pathological arrangements that confuse readers.
UWC generates QR codes with the qrcode library and scans them from images with jsQR — both run entirely in your browser, so sensitive payloads (WiFi passwords, TOTP seeds) never leave the device.

vcard.title: vCard
vcard.tagline: The contact card that predates smartphones.

meta.title: vCard format — history, VCF structure, QR contacts
meta.description: vCard explained: Versit consortium 1995, VCF properties and parameters, encoding rules — and free vCard ↔ JSON conversion in your browser.

vcard.history:
vCard was created in 1995 by the Versit consortium (Apple, AT&T, IBM, Siemens) as electronic business cards for PDAs. Version 3.0 (1998) stabilized the property model everyone uses; 4.0 (2011) refined it.
Its second life came via QR codes — WiFi passwords aside, 'scan my contact' cards are vCards in disguise.
vcard.how:
A VCF file is a list of properties: `BEGIN:VCARD`, then `FN:Name`, `TEL;TYPE=CELL:+1234567890`, `EMAIL:...`, ending with `END:VCARD`. Parameters after semicolons qualify properties; long lines fold at 75 chars with continuation spaces; special characters escape with backslashes.
Repeated properties (multiple phones, addresses) naturally map to JSON arrays — which is exactly what UWC's converter preserves, along with TYPE parameters.

ical.title: iCal
ical.tagline: Calendar invites as plain text since 1998.

meta.title: iCalendar format — history, ICS structure, RRULE
meta.description: iCalendar (ICS) explained: vCalendar heritage, RFC 5545, events and recurrence rules, timezone gotchas — and free iCal ↔ JSON conversion.

ical.history: iCalendar grew out of vCalendar (1996, again the Versit crowd) and was standardized as RFC 2445 in 1998, updated by RFC 5545 in 2009. Every calendar invite you've ever accepted — Outlook, Google, Apple — traveled as an .ics attachment.
ical.how:
Same property model as vCard: `BEGIN:VEVENT ... END:VEVENT` blocks with DTSTART/DTEND, SUMMARY, UID. The powerful part is recurrence: `RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE` describes infinite schedules compactly.
Timezones are the eternal trap: floating times vs UTC vs TZID references cause most calendar bugs ever filed.
UWC parses the practical RFC subset — events, dates, folding, escaping — and maps repeating properties to JSON arrays.

geojson.title: GeoJSON
geojson.tagline: Maps as JSON: points, lines, polygons.

meta.title: GeoJSON format — history, geometry types, KML/GPX conversion
meta.description: GeoJSON explained: 2008 spec, RFC 7946, Point/LineString/Polygon geometries, coordinate order — and free GeoJSON ↔ KML/GPX/CSV conversion.

geojson.history: GeoJSON crystallized in 2008 from a grassroots mailing-list effort to standardize geographic JSON; RFC 7946 (2016) finalized it. It dethroned heavier XML formats (KML, GML) across the mapping world — Leaflet, Mapbox, OpenStreetMap tooling all breathe GeoJSON.
geojson.how:
A FeatureCollection wraps Features; each has `geometry` (Point, LineString, Polygon, Multi* variants) and arbitrary `properties`. Coordinates are [longitude, latitude] — order matters and trips everyone up at least once.
Polygons close their rings (first point = last point) and follow winding-order conventions for holes.
UWC converts GeoJSON to KML (Google Earth), GPX (GPS devices) and CSV (spreadsheets) — all transformations run locally.

pdf.title: PDF
pdf.tagline: Paper, but virtual: documents that look the same everywhere.

meta.title: PDF format — history, internals, text extraction
meta.description: PDF explained: Adobe 1993, the Camelot project, page description language, why text extraction is hard — and free PDF → text conversion.

pdf.history:
PDF grew out of Adobe's Camelot project (1991) by John Warnock: a universal format that would preserve document layout on any machine — 'paper transported over wires'. Version 1.0 shipped in 1993; Adobe kept it proprietary until 2008, when it was released to ISO as an open standard.
The gamble paid off beyond expectations: today PDF is how contracts, articles, books and receipts travel.
pdf.how:
A PDF is not a stream of text — it's a page *description* language. Pages contain positioned glyphs (often with custom embedded fonts and encodings), vector graphics and raster images. Text is drawn, not written: 'place glyph #42 at (100, 200)'.
That's why extracting text is genuinely hard: the extractor must reverse glyph mappings back into Unicode, deal with ligatures, hyphenation and reading order. UWC uses pdfjs-dist (the engine behind Firefox's viewer) to walk pages and reconstruct readable text.

cta.text: Extract text from PDF documents — processed server-side, nothing stored.

docx.title: DOCX
docx.tagline: Word documents unzipped: XML all the way down.

meta.title: DOCX format — history, OOXML structure, HTML/TXT conversion
meta.description: DOCX explained: Office Open XML since 2007, document.xml structure, runs and paragraphs, converting DOCX to HTML or plain text without Word.

docx.history:
DOCX replaced the binary .doc in Office 2007 as part of Office Open XML (ECMA-376). The move was partly forced: governments and competitors demanded open formats, and a zip of XML was Microsoft's answer — proprietary in spirit but at least parseable by anyone.
It became the default business-document format worldwide, for better and worse.
docx.how:
A DOCX is a ZIP whose heart is word/document.xml: paragraphs (〈w:p〉) contain runs (〈w:r〉), runs contain text (〈w:t〉) with formatting properties. Styles, numbering, headers and images live in sibling parts linked by relationships.
Because the content model maps cleanly to HTML (paragraph → 〈p〉, run → 〈span〉, bold → 〈strong〉), DOCX→HTML conversion is nearly mechanical — that's what UWC does via mammoth, plus a plain-text mode that strips everything but words.

xlsx.title: XLSX
xlsx.tagline: Spreadsheets as a zip of XML.

meta.title: XLSX format — history, OOXML structure, CSV/JSON conversion
meta.description: XLSX explained: Office Open XML, why it's a zip of tables and styles, compatibility — and free XLSX ↔ CSV/JSON conversion.

xlsx.history:
XLSX arrived with Office 2007 as part of Office Open XML — Microsoft moved binary formats (.xls, .doc, .ppt) to 'a zip with XML inside', partially opening the specs under competitive and government pressure. Since 2008 it's standardized as ISO/IEC ECMA-376.
Today it's understood not only by Excel but by LibreOffice, Google Sheets, Numbers and half the BI tooling.
xlsx.how:
Physically an .xlsx is a ZIP archive: workbook.xml describes sheets, sheet1.xml stores cells (referencing shared strings in sharedStrings.xml), styles.xml holds formatting. That's why a corrupted xlsx can sometimes be 'repaired' by unzipping it.
Cells are typed: numbers, strings (via shared-string indices), dates (numbers with a format), formulas stored alongside their last computed value.
UWC reads XLSX via exceljs (MIT) on the server and outputs CSV or JSON — files are processed in memory and never stored.

pptx.title: PPTX
pptx.tagline: PowerPoint presentations are also zip with XML inside.

meta.title: PPTX format — history, OOXML structure, content extraction
meta.description: PPTX explained: Office Open XML for presentations, slides as XML parts, extracting text and images — working with PPTX without PowerPoint.

pptx.history: PPTX replaced binary .ppt along with the rest of Office 2007's move to Office Open XML (ECMA-376). Like DOCX/XLSX, it made presentation content accessible to third-party tools — previously that required PowerPoint itself.
pptx.how:
Inside: a ZIP where each slide is its own XML file (slide1.xml, slide2.xml…) under ppt/slides, text lives in 〈a:t〉 runs, images are media files linked through relationship files. Themes and slide masters describe appearance.
So extracting all text and images from a PPTX is just walking the archive — exactly what UWC does: slides are parsed server-side, content is returned without installing Office.

epub.title: EPUB
epub.tagline: An e-book as a website in an archive.

meta.title: EPUB format — history, structure, book conversion
meta.description: EPUB explained: IDPF/W3C e-book standard, XHTML chapters in a ZIP container, reflowable layout — converting EPUB without Calibre.

epub.history:
EPUB emerged in 2007 from the Open eBook Publication Structure effort by IDPF; since 2017 the standard is maintained by W3C (after merging with IDPF). Version 3 dropped legacy XML in favor of plain HTML5.
It's the most widespread e-book format — everything understands it except Kindle (Amazon keeps pushing its own formats).
epub.how:
An EPUB is a ZIP with mandatory META-INF/container.xml pointing to the OPF manifest: chapter list (XHTML), metadata, reading order, CSS. Readers render chapters as web pages with reflowable layout — changing font size re-flows text instead of zooming.
Consequence: converting EPUB is essentially working with HTML. UWC uses exactly that — chapters are unpacked and converted like ordinary HTML.

rtf.title: RTF
rtf.tagline: Rich Text Format: a document you can read as source.

meta.title: RTF format — history, control words, where it survives
meta.description: RTF explained: Microsoft's 1987 text format, groups and control words, why it still lives in clipboards — and RTF conversion.

rtf.history:
RTF was created by Microsoft in 1987 to exchange documents across platforms and Word versions. Paradox: proprietary in spirit yet fully textual — an RTF file opens in Notepad and reads almost like TeX.
Its niche today is the clipboard (formatted copy-paste between apps often goes through RTF) and embedded editors that don't want a full DOCX parser.
rtf.how:
RTF mixes text with backslash control words: «\b» starts bold, «\par» ends a paragraph, groups wrap in braces. Encodings are handled with escapes («\'e9», «\u1055?»).
The format is verbose (documents balloon versus DOCX) but trivially streamable: a parser is a finite-state machine — no zip, no XML.
UWC strips formatting and extracts clean text from RTF right in your browser.

cta.text: RTF → clean text with no formatting residue — local and instant.

rot13.title: ROT13
rot13.tagline: The cipher that has hidden spoilers for forty years.

meta.title: ROT13 — cipher history, Usenet culture, self-inverse property
meta.description: ROT13 explained: Caesar shift by 13, Usenet spoiler culture, why encoding and decoding are the same operation — and an instant ROT13 converter.

rot13.history:
ROT13 is a Caesar cipher with shift 13, popularized on 80s Usenet: movie spoilers and puzzle answers were hidden behind it — 'don't read below, it's ROT13'. Nobody took it seriously as encryption; it was a cultural contract meaning 'you were warned'.
Choosing exactly 13 was laziness at its finest: Latin has 26 letters, so applying ROT13 twice returns the original text — encode and decode are the same operation.
rot13.how:
Each letter shifts 13 positions through the alphabet: A→N, B→O, … N→A. Case is preserved; digits and punctuation untouched.
The math: shifting by 13 twice = shifting by 26 ≡ 0 mod 26. Hence self-inversion — one function does both directions.
UWC applies ROT13 to Latin letters in your browser; for Cyrillic there's keyboard-layout conversion and translit in neighboring converters.

sql-dump.title: SQL dumps

meta.title: SQL dumps — structure, INSERT parsing, JSON conversion
meta.description: SQL dump files explained: CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements, mysqldump/pg_dump output, parsing without a database — and SQL dump ↔ JSON conversion.

sql-dump.history: As long as relational databases existed, people needed to move data out of them. Dump utilities (mysqldump, pg_dump, sqlite .dump) emit plain-text SQL — a de-facto interchange format nobody formally standardized but everyone depends on.
sql-dump.how:
A dump contains DDL (`CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name TEXT)` — column names live here) and DML (`INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Ann'), (2, NULL)` — the rows).
Parsing it properly means handling quoted strings with escaped quotes (`''`), NULL literals, numeric and boolean literals — no actual database required.
UWC regex-parses the dump structure in pure JS (no GPL SQLite bindings), reconstructing typed rows as JSON or CSV.

tsv.title: TSV
tsv.tagline: CSV with a tab instead of a comma — built for shells.

meta.title: TSV — history, why tabs, conversion to CSV/Markdown
meta.description: TSV explained: tab-separated values, why terminals and awk love them, the quoting problem they avoid — and TSV ↔ CSV/Markdown conversion in your browser.

tsv.history:
Tab-separated values are CSV's quieter sibling. When Unix tools like awk, cut and sort needed a column format, the tab was the natural delimiter: it never appears inside text, so there is nothing to escape.
That single property made TSV the lingua franca of data plumbing — paste, join, and every shell pipeline speak it natively. Spreadsheets import it too; Excel just calls it "Text (tab-delimited)".
tsv.how:
Mechanically TSV is CSV with delimiter "\t". The killer advantage: a tab almost never shows up in real data, so you drop the entire quoting machinery — no doubled quotes, no escaping rules.
The downside is human eyes: tabs are invisible, so misaligned columns are maddening to debug by hand. UWC converts TSV ↔ CSV (re-introducing quotes) and TSV → Markdown tables losslessly, entirely client-side.

cta.text: TSV to CSV for spreadsheets, or straight into a Markdown table — computed locally.

ini.title: INI
ini.tagline: The config format that refused to die.

meta.title: INI files — history, sections, where they still hide
meta.description: INI explained: the Windows 3.x config format, [sections] and key=value, why it survived in git config and Python — and INI ↔ JSON/YAML/TOML conversion.

ini.history:
INI traces back to MS-DOS and Windows 3.x, where "initialization" files stored program settings in plain text. There was never a formal spec — every app bent the rules a little, and that casualness is exactly why INI spread everywhere.
It outlived its era: git uses it (.git/config), Python still ships configparser, and PHP php.ini is INI to this day. Simplicity beat standardization.
ini.how:
Structure is flat sections in brackets — [database] — followed by key=value lines. Comments start with ; or #. Values are usually strings; typeless by default.
The lack of nesting is INI's ceiling: you fake hierarchies with section names like [server.cache]. UWC maps sections to objects and round-trips INI through JSON, YAML and TOML without losing the tree.

cta.text: INI → JSON/YAML/TOML for scripts and docs — parsed in your browser, nothing uploaded.

hjson.title: HJSON

meta.title: HJSON — history, comments in JSON, readable configs
meta.description: HJSON explained: the "Human JSON" superset, why comments and unquoted keys matter, how it compiles to strict JSON — and HJSON ↔ JSON conversion.

hjson.history:
HJSON ("Human JSON") grew out of the same frustration that spawned JSON5 and HJSON's siblings: real config files want comments and relaxed quoting, but strict JSON forbids both. HJSON picked the pragmatic middle ground.
It never tried to replace JSON — it compiles down to it. Editors and config loaders decode HJSON, then hand standard JSON to the rest of the stack.
hjson.how:
HJSON relaxes the rules: comments with # or //, unquoted keys, unquoted string values, and multi-line strings. Whitespace is significant like in YAML, but there are no indentation traps.
The conversion is a straight parse → re-serialize to JSON. UWC does HJSON ↔ JSON both ways in the browser, so you can author comfortably and ship strict JSON.

cta.text: Write forgiving HJSON, get strict JSON — or the other way around, locally.

properties.title: Properties

meta.title: Java .properties — history, escaping, UTF-8
meta.description: Properties files explained: the Java config format, ISO-8859-1 escaping, dotted keys, why Spring still uses them — and Properties ↔ JSON conversion.

properties.history:
Java introduced .properties in the mid-90s as its built-in configuration store, shipped with the JDK's java.util.Properties. It became the default for localization bundles (messages_en.properties) and app config across the ecosystem.
Frameworks from Spring to Maven still read it. Despite newer formats, properties files remain the lowest-common-denominator config in the JVM world.
properties.how:
Syntax is key=value (or key:value, whitespace allowed). Lines starting with # or ! are comments. Keys are often dotted namespaces: db.url, db.user.
The historical gotcha: the classic format escaped non-ASCII as \uXXXX (ISO-8859-1), so raw UTF-8 broke. UWC parses the structure and maps dotted keys into a nested JSON object, in your browser.

env.title: ENV

meta.title: .env files — history, twelve-factor config, secrets
meta.description: ENV files explained: the dotenv format, twelve-factor app config, why secrets live in the environment — and ENV ↔ JSON conversion.

env.history:
ENV files come from the dotenv pattern, popularized by Heroku's twelve-factor app methodology around 2010: config belongs in the environment, not in code. A .env file is just a local dump of those variables.
Tools like Docker Compose and countless CLIs read .env on startup. It is the simplest possible secret-passing mechanism — and the easiest to leak if committed to git.
env.how:
Each line is KEY=VALUE. Values may be quoted; # starts a comment. No sections, no nesting — it is a flat key→string map by design.
UWC parses .env into a JSON object (quotes stripped, comments dropped) and can serialize JSON back into a .env, all client-side. Nothing leaves the browser.

jsonp.title: JSONP

meta.title: JSONP — history, the padding trick, why it died
meta.description: JSONP explained: the pre-CORS callback hack, how 〈script〉 tags bypassed same-origin, why it is obsolete — and JSONP ↔ JSON conversion.

jsonp.history:
JSONP ("JSON with Padding") was the workaround for the browser same-origin policy before CORS existed. A 〈script〉 tag can load anything cross-domain, so APIs wrapped JSON in a function call: callback(﹛"a":1﹜).
It powered early AJAX against third-party APIs (Twitter, Flickr). Once CORS arrived, JSONP became a security liability and faded — but legacy endpoints still serve it.
jsonp.how:
A JSONP response is not JSON: it is JavaScript of the form fn(〈json〉). The "padding" is the callback name. To use it you inject a 〈script〉 and define fn to catch the data.
Converting means stripping the wrapper to recover pure JSON, or re-wrapping JSON with a callback. UWC does both in the browser — handy when a stubborn old API only speaks JSONP.

markdown.title: Markdown
markdown.tagline: Formatting you can read as plain text.

meta.title: Markdown — history, CommonMark, where it won
meta.description: Markdown explained: John Gruber's 2004 plain-text formatting, the # and ** conventions, CommonMark standardization — and Markdown ↔ HTML conversion.

markdown.history:
Markdown was created in 2004 by John Gruber with Aaron Swartz, to let people "write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format" that converts to HTML. The pitch was radical: source should be readable as-is.
It conquered the web sideways — GitHub, Reddit, Stack Overflow, and every docs site (including this one) render Markdown. What began as a blog tool became the documentation lingua franca.
markdown.how:
Conventions are intuitive: # heading, **bold**, *italic*, - list, > quote, [text](url) link, `code`. The formatting is a thin layer over plain text you can still read raw.
The catch is ambiguity — dozens of dialects (GitHub Flavored, CommonMark). UWC converts Markdown ↔ HTML both ways client-side, handling the common subset without a server.

html.title: HTML
html.tagline: The markup that built the web.

meta.title: HTML — history, tags, the living standard
meta.description: HTML explained: from Tim Berners-Lee's 1991 proposal to the living standard, tags and the DOM, why it is everywhere — and HTML ↔ Markdown conversion.

html.history:
HTML was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 as the publishing language of the World Wide Web, derived from CERN's SGML. Version 2 (1995) and the browser wars of the late 90s shaped it; HTML5 (2014) made it a "living standard" that never freezes.
It is the only format every browser speaks — which is why almost everything else (email, ebooks, help files) is either HTML or a wrapper around it.
html.how:
HTML is a tree of tags: 〈p〉paragraph〈/p〉, 〈a href〉link〈/a〉, 〈h1〉heading〈/h1〉. Browsers parse it into the DOM, a live object model, tolerating errors gracefully (a missing 〈/p〉 just closes itself).
Going HTML → Markdown is a lossy simplification: structure and links survive, but styling and scripts are dropped. UWC does the round-trip in your browser for clean, readable Markdown.

txt.title: TXT
txt.tagline: The only format every computer understands.

meta.title: Plain text (.txt) — history, encoding, the universal format
meta.description: TXT explained: the humblest file of all, encodings from ASCII to UTF-8, why plain text outlives everything — and TXT ↔ DOCX/PDF conversion.

txt.history:
Plain text is not really a "format" — it is the absence of one. A .txt file is just bytes interpreted as characters, readable by every operating system since the 1960s. Its superpower is longevity: no app, no version, no license required.
Everything else is a bet that some software will still exist to read it. TXT is the fallback that always wins.
txt.how:
The only real question is encoding: ASCII (7-bit), Latin-1, Windows-1251, or UTF-8 (the modern default that handles every script). A .txt with the wrong encoding shows mojibake.
UWC converts plain text to DOCX and PDF (and back from DOCX/PDF to text) on the server, preserving your words while you stay in the browser.

base32.title: Base32

meta.title: Base32 — history, Crockford vs RFC 4648, human-safe encoding
meta.description: Base32 explained: why it drops ambiguous characters, RFC 4648 vs Crockford alphabets, where it is used (TOTP, Tor) — and instant Base32 encode/decode.

base32.history:
Base32 was standardized in RFC 4648 (2006) to fix Base64's weakness for humans: Base64 uses 0/O, 1/l/I which get confused when read aloud or copied. Base32 restricts itself to A–Z and 2–7, avoiding those glyphs entirely.
That made it the choice for things typed or spoken: TOTP authenticator secrets, Bitcoin/Tor onion addresses, and DNS labels that must survive case-insensitive systems.
base32.how:
Like Base64, it groups bits — here 5 bits per character, 8 characters per 40-bit block. Output is ~20% bigger than Base64 but safe to read.
A padding character "=" fills the tail. Crockford's variant drops padding and ambiguous chars (I,L,O,U) entirely. UWC encodes/decodes Base32 in your browser, UTF-8 safe.

base36.title: Base36
base36.tagline: Digits and letters, the URL-friendly base.

meta.title: Base36 — history, case-insensitive IDs, short links
meta.description: Base36 explained: the 0-9A-Z alphabet, why it shortens IDs, comparison with Base62/Base64 — and instant Base36 encode/decode.

base36.history:
Base36 uses the ten digits and twenty-six letters — exactly the characters in the English alphanumeric set. Because it is case-insensitive, it is safe in places that mangle case: URLs, file names, and human-shared IDs.
You have seen it in YouTube video IDs and URL shorteners, where a number like 12345678 becomes the shorter, friendlier "7CLZI".
base36.how:
It is positional like any base: each digit carries 36^n. Converting a byte string to Base36 is straightforward grouping of bits into 5.17-bit chunks — implementations just map values 0–35 to 0-9 then A-Z.
UWC turns raw bytes into Base36 and back entirely client-side. For case-sensitive, higher-density IDs, Base62 (adds lowercase) is the sibling.

base62.title: Base62

meta.title: Base62 — history, URL-safe IDs, vs Base64
meta.description: Base62 explained: the 0-9A-Za-z alphabet, why it beats Base64 for IDs, use in shorteners — and instant Base62 encode/decode.

base62.history:
Base62 takes Base36 and adds lowercase letters, using the full 62-character alphanumeric set. It is the sweet spot for unique IDs: denser than Base36, yet still free of +, / and = that make Base64 hostile to URLs.
URL shorteners (bit.ly), YouTube (mixed case IDs), and Snowflake-style primary keys all lean on Base62 to pack big integers into short, copy-paste-safe strings.
base62.how:
Each character encodes log2(62) ≈ 5.95 bits. Conversion is repeated division by 62, mapping remainders to 0-9A-Za-z. No padding needed, no reserved characters.
UWC encodes bytes to Base62 and decodes them back in your browser. It is the go-to when you need compactness without URL-escaping headaches.

ascii85.title: Ascii85

meta.title: Ascii85 — history, Adobe/PostScript, btoa vs RFC 1924
meta.description: Ascii85 explained: the 85-character encoding from PostScript, how it beats Base64 density, where it hides (PDF) — and instant Ascii85 encode/decode.

ascii85.history:
Ascii85 (a.k.a. Base85) was invented by Paul Riddle for the btoa utility and adopted by Adobe in PostScript and PDF. The idea: 85 printable characters is enough to represent 32 bits (4 bytes) in just 5 characters.
You meet it inside every PDF stream — encoded image and font data is wrapped in 〈~ ... ~〉 Ascii85 delimiters before being decompressed.
ascii85.how:
Take 4 bytes (32 bits) and express them in base 85, emitting 5 characters. That is ~25% overhead versus Base64's 33% — denser, but the alphabet includes trickier punctuation.
Variants differ: Adobe uses ! to ~, RFC 1924 (IPv6) uses a different alphabet, and "Z" often stands for four zero bytes. UWC handles the common encodings entirely offline.

hex.title: Hex

meta.title: Hexadecimal — history, bytes as 0-9A-F, where it lives
meta.description: Hex explained: base-16 since the 1950s, why it maps perfectly to bytes, use in colors and crypto — and Hex encode/decode plus Hex ↔ RGB.

hex.history:
Hexadecimal (base 16) became standard in computing because one byte is exactly two hex digits: 8 bits = 2^8 = 256 = 16^2. That 1:1 mapping between nibbles and characters made it the natural way to "see" memory.
From debuggers dumping RAM to MAC addresses, hash outputs and color codes (#ff0000), hex is how machines show their innards to humans.
hex.how:
Digits 0–9 then A–F stand for 10–15. A byte like 255 is FF. Converting is grouping bits into 4-bit nibbles. Whitespace or "0x" prefixes are usually tolerated.
UWC encodes text to hex and decodes it back, and bridges hex with RGB so you can flip between #ff0000 and rgb(255,0,0) in the browser.

quoted-printable.title: Quoted-Printable

meta.title: Quoted-Printable — history, MIME email, soft line breaks
meta.description: Quoted-Printable explained: the MIME encoding for mostly-ASCII email, = and soft breaks, why it stays readable — and instant QP encode/decode.

quoted-printable.history:
Quoted-Printable (QP) was defined in RFC 2045 as part of MIME, the standard that taught email to carry attachments and non-ASCII text. The design goal was clever: leave ordinary ASCII mostly readable while escaping the rest.
That is why a QP email is still legible in a raw "View Source" — unlike Base64, where everything turns to gibberish.
quoted-printable.how:
Printable ASCII passes through unchanged; anything else is encoded as =XX (two hex digits, e.g. =E2=82=AC for €). An "=" at line end is a "soft break" continuing the line.
Lines are capped at 76 characters with a soft break. UWC encodes and decodes QP entirely in your browser — useful when inspecting raw email.

uuencode.title: Uuencode
uuencode.tagline: The 1980s way to mail a binary.

meta.title: Uuencode — history, Usenet binaries, begin/end blocks
meta.description: Uuencode explained: the pre-MIME binary-in-email trick, begin 644 headers, why Base64 replaced it — and instant uuencode/uudecode.

uuencode.history:
Uuencode ("Unix-to-Unix encode") appeared in the early 1980s to send binaries over UUCP and Usenet, where only text could travel. It wrapped files in begin 644 / end blocks with permission bits.
It predates MIME and Base64 by years. Once email standardized on Base64, uuencode became a historical curiosity — but old archives and Unix folklore still hold it.
uuencode.how:
It encodes 3 bytes into 4 characters by adding 32 (space becomes the smallest value). The begin line carries the file mode (e.g. 644) and name; end closes it.
The format is famously fragile: a single corrupted line breaks the rest. UWC still uuencodes and uudecodes it for completeness, entirely offline.

idn.title: Punycode / IDN
idn.tagline: How domains speak Arabic and Cyrillic.

meta.title: Punycode & IDN — history, internationalized domains, xn--
meta.description: Punycode explained: encoding Unicode domains into ASCII, the xn-- prefix, why it prevents homograph attacks — and IDN encode/decode.

idn.history:
The Domain Name System only speaks ASCII, but the world does not. IDN (Internationalized Domain Names) solved this in the early 2000s with Punycode (RFC 3492), translating Unicode labels into ASCII that DNS accepts.
So "россия.рф" becomes "xn--h1alffa9f.xn--p1ai". The "xn--" prefix marks a Punycode label — and it is also why lookalike "homograph" phishing (cyrillic а vs latin a) is a real threat.
idn.how:
Punycode isolates the non-ASCII part and encodes it as a base-36-ish sequence after a "-" delimiter, with the ASCII prefix kept verbatim. Decoding reverses it.
UWC converts between human-readable IDN and its ASCII Punycode form in your browser — handy for verifying what a suspicious domain actually is.

jwt.title: JWT

meta.title: JWT — history, the three Base64 segments, JOSE
meta.description: JWT explained: JSON Web Tokens, header.payload.signature, why the middle is just Base64, security caveats — and instant JWT decode.

jwt.history:
JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) emerged from the JOSE working group around 2014 as a compact, URL-safe way to carry claims between parties. It became the default auth token for SPAs and APIs overnight.
Its appeal: self-contained — a server signs a payload and the client just presents it. No session lookup needed. Its danger: a misconfigured "none" algorithm or weak secret leaks everything.
jwt.how:
A JWT is three Base64url segments joined by dots: header.algorithm.payload.claims.signature. Only the signature is opaque; the header and payload are plain Base64url you can decode and read.
UWC decodes the header and payload client-side so you can inspect claims (sub, exp, iat) — it never verifies or forges signatures, keeping your secrets local.

sha256.title: SHA-256
sha256.tagline: The fingerprint behind half the internet.

meta.title: SHA-256 — history, the SHA-2 family, where it secures
meta.description: SHA-256 explained: NIST's 2001 hash, the SHA-2 family, why it secures Bitcoin and TLS — and instant SHA-256 hashing.

sha256.history:
SHA-256 is part of SHA-2, published by NIST in 2001 after SHA-1 started showing weaknesses. It produces a 256-bit (32-byte) digest. When SHA-1 was finally broken in 2017, SHA-256 was already everywhere.
It underpins TLS certificates, Git commit hashes (via SHA-1's successor plans), Bitcoin proof-of-work, and integrity checks for every download you verify.
sha256.how:
SHA-256 is a one-way function: any input — a password, a file — maps to a fixed 32-byte fingerprint. Change one bit and the hash completely changes (the avalanche effect).
You cannot reverse it, but you can verify: hash your file and compare. UWC computes SHA-256 in your browser using the Web Crypto API — no upload, no server.

md5.title: MD5
md5.tagline: The fast hash that should not secure anything.

meta.title: MD5 — history, the 1996 break, why it still appears
meta.description: MD5 explained: Rivest's 1991 hash, how it was shattered by collisions, why it lingers for checksums — and instant MD5 hashing.

md5.history:
MD5 (Message Digest 5) was designed by Ron Rivest in 1991 as a fast 128-bit hash. For years it was the default for passwords and integrity. Then in 2004 researchers published practical collisions — two different files with the same MD5.
That killed its security use. Yet it survives for non-adversarial checksums (file dedup, etag hints) precisely because it is fast and short.
md5.how:
Like SHA, MD5 is one-way: text in, 16-byte digest out, rendered as 32 hex chars. But collisions are cheap to manufacture, so an attacker can forge a matching hash.
UWC computes MD5 in the browser for quick integrity checks — never trust it for passwords or signatures. For that, use SHA-256.

crc32.title: CRC32
crc32.tagline: The checksum that catches cable noise.

meta.title: CRC32 — history, cyclic redundancy, ZIP and PNG
meta.description: CRC32 explained: cyclic redundancy checks, why they catch transmission errors, where they live (ZIP, PNG, Ethernet) — and instant CRC32.

crc32.history:
CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) was formalized by W. Wesley Peterson in 1961 for reliable data transmission. CRC32 — a 32-bit variant — became ubiquitous in networking and storage: Ethernet frames, ZIP, PNG, and gzip all embed one.
It was never meant to stop attackers, only to catch accidental corruption: a flipped bit on a cable, a bad sector on disk.
crc32.how:
CRC treats the message as a polynomial and divides it by a fixed generator, keeping the remainder as the checksum. A tiny change in input flips many bits of the CRC — great at spotting errors.
Crucially, CRC is not cryptographic: it is trivial to craft a collision. UWC computes CRC32 in your browser for integrity checks, never for security.

iban.title: IBAN
iban.tagline: Bank accounts with a built-in checksum.

meta.title: IBAN — history, the ISO 13616 standard, MOD-97 check
meta.description: IBAN explained: International Bank Account Numbers, the 34-char format, the MOD-97 checksum that catches typos — and IBAN validate/format.

iban.history:
IBAN (International Bank Account Number) was created by the European Committee for Banking Standards in the 1990s and standardized as ISO 13616, to make cross-border payments reliable. Before it, every country had its own account format and transfers failed constantly.
Today over 80 countries use IBAN, from Germany's DE to Russia's RU and Saudi Arabia's SA. The US still mostly does not.
iban.how:
An IBAN is up to 34 characters: a two-letter country code, two check digits, then the national account. The magic is MOD-97: rearrange and treat it as a number, divide by 97, and the remainder must be 1 — that catches almost all typos.
UWC validates and reformats IBANs (grouping into fours) in your browser, checking the checksum without sending anything.

roman.title: Roman numerals
roman.tagline: I, II, III, IV — counting like the Romans.

meta.title: Roman numerals — history, subtractive notation, modern use
meta.description: Roman numerals explained: the ancient additive/subtractive system, why 4 is IV not IIII, where they survive (clocks, movies) — and Roman ↔ Arabic conversion.

roman.history:
Romans used a base-10 system with letters: I, V, X, L, C, D, M. It served an empire for centuries without zero or place value. The modern "subtractive" shortcuts (IV for 4, IX for 9) were formalized in the Middle Ages.
They refuse to die: movie copyright years (MMXXIV), clock faces, book volume numbers, and Super Bowl titles all use them as a stylistic choice.
roman.how:
Values add left to right, but a smaller numeral before a larger subtracts (IX = 10−1). There are rules: never repeat V, L, D; subtract only I, X, C and only from the next two ranks.
Valid range is 1–3999 (no symbol for 5000+). UWC converts Roman ↔ Arabic both ways in your browser, rejecting malformed strings.

mac.title: MAC address
mac.tagline: The serial number burned into your NIC.

meta.title: MAC address — history, the 48-bit identifier, OUI
meta.description: MAC addresses explained: the hardware address of network cards, the 48-bit structure, OUI vendors, the colon/dash/cisco formats — and MAC formatting.

mac.history:
The MAC (Media Access Control) address was defined by the IEEE 802 standards in the 1980s as the hardware identity of a network interface. It is burned into the card at manufacture — your device's permanent name on the local network.
Xerox, later the IEEE, handed out the first 24 bits (the OUI) to vendors: look up "00:1A:2B" and you know it is, say, a specific manufacturer.
mac.how:
A MAC is 48 bits, written as six groups of two hex digits: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The format varies — colons (Unix), dashes (Windows), or dotted cisco (001a.2b3c.4d5e).
The 7th bit (locally administered) flips when software spoofs an address. UWC reformats MACs between styles in your browser without sending data.

color.title: HEX / RGB / HSL
color.tagline: Three ways to name the same color.

meta.title: Color models — history, HEX vs RGB vs HSL, CSS
meta.description: Color formats explained: hexadecimal and RGB triplets, HSL's human-friendly hue, why designers prefer HSL — and HEX ↔ RGB ↔ HSL conversion.

color.history:
Screens mix red, green and blue light, so RGB is the native model: three 0–255 intensities. Hex is just RGB written in base-16 for compactness in code. HSL (Hue, Saturation, Lightness) came later as the designer-friendly view.
CSS supports all three; pick Hex for copy-paste, RGB for clarity, HSL when you want "a lighter shade of this hue" without math.
color.how:
RGB(r,g,b) names the three channels directly. HEX collapses them to #rrggbb. HSL describes a color by hue angle (0–360), saturation and lightness — intuitive to tweak.
Conversion is fixed math: HSL→RGB→HEX are pure functions. UWC converts any of the three to the others in your browser, ideal for quick theming.

avif.tagline: The modern image format that crushes JPEG.

meta.title: AVIF — history, AV1 video codec, why it is small
meta.description: AVIF explained: the AV1-based image format from Netflix/AOMedia, royalty-free compression, HDR support — and AVIF → PNG/JPEG conversion.

avif.history:
AVIF (AV1 Image File Format) was released in 2019 by the Alliance for Open Media (Google, Netflix, Amazon, Microsoft) as the still-image cousin of the AV1 video codec. The mission: royalty-free compression that beats JPEG and even HEIC.
Backed by every major browser by 2022, AVIF is now the go-to for web images that must be tiny without looking bad.
avif.how:
Technically AVIF reuses AV1 intra-frame coding — the same tech that shrinks 4K video — applied to a single picture. It supports HDR, wide color gamut, transparency, and lossless modes.

tiff.tagline: The archival format that refuses to compress away.

meta.title: TIFF — history, Aldus/Adobe, lossless archiving
meta.description: TIFF explained: the Tagged Image File Format, layers and metadata, why scanners and publishers love it — and TIFF → PNG/JPEG conversion.

tiff.history:
TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) was created in 1986 by Aldus (later absorbed by Adobe) for desktop publishing and scanners. Its tag-based design let it grow features without breaking old readers.
It remains the format of choice for print prepress, medical imaging (DICOM wraps it), and archival scans where quality is non-negotiable.
tiff.how:
TIFF stores image data in "directories" of tagged fields — resolution, compression, color profile, layers. It can be uncompressed (lossless) or use LZW/Zip, and supports 16-bit and multi-page documents.
Its flexibility makes files heavy and support uneven on the web. UWC converts TIFF → PNG/JPEG server-side, keeping your machine light.

bmp.title: BMP

meta.title: BMP — history, device-independent bitmap, why files are huge
meta.description: BMP explained: the Windows bitmap format, raw pixels with no compression, where it survives — and BMP → PNG/JPEG conversion.

bmp.history:
BMP (Bitmap) shipped with Windows 3.0 in 1990 as the Device-Independent Bitmap, letting apps draw without knowing the screen hardware. It was simple: a header, then raw pixels bottom-to-top.
Its lack of compression made it the reliable interchange format of early Windows — but also meant a modest photo ballooned to megabytes. PNG and JPEG quickly took its crown.
bmp.how:
A BMP is essentially a header (width, height, bit depth) followed by uncompressed pixel data. No entropy coding, so decoding is trivial and instant.
That simplicity is why BMPs still appear in legacy systems and icons. UWC converts BMP → PNG/JPEG server-side, shrinking the file without loss of visible quality.

cur.title: CUR

meta.title: CUR — history, Windows cursor format, hot spot
meta.description: CUR explained: the Windows cursor format, how it differs from ICO (hot spot), where it lives — and CUR → PNG/JPEG conversion.

cur.history:
CUR is the cursor sibling of ICO, also from early Windows. It stores the same multi-resolution bitmaps but adds one field ICO lacks: the "hot spot" — the exact pixel that counts as the click point.
You meet CUR in .cur files used for custom mouse pointers on the web and in Windows themes. Functionally it is ICO with a pointer.
cur.how:
Like ICO, CUR is a container of small images; the extra hot-spot coordinates (x,y) tell the OS where the arrow "tip" is. Without it, every cursor would click from its top-left corner.

ppm.title: PPM
ppm.tagline: The easiest image format to parse by hand.

meta.title: PPM — history, the Netpbm portable format, raw pixels
meta.description: PPM explained: the Portable Pixmap from Netpbm, dead-simple ASCII/binary pixels, why it is loved in teaching — and PPM → PNG/JPEG conversion.

ppm.history:
PPM (Portable Pixmap) is part of the Netpbm toolkit's "portable anymap" family from the late 1980s — PBM (1-bit), PGM (gray), PPM (color). The goal was interchange between Unix image tools, not compression.
Its charm is pedagogical: you can read and write a PPM with a few lines of C. It is the "hello world" of image formats.
ppm.how:
A PPM is a magic number (P3 for ASCII, P6 for binary), then width, height, max-value, then raw pixel triples. No compression, no metadata — just numbers.
That verbosity is why it never hit the web, but it is perfect for pipelines and learning. UWC converts PPM → PNG/JPEG server-side.

meta.title: TGA — history, Truevision Targa, game textures
meta.description: TGA explained: the Truevision Targa format, alpha channels, its game-era popularity — and TGA → PNG/JPEG conversion.

tga.history:
TGA (Targa) was created by Truevision in 1984 for their TARGA graphics cards, aimed at professional video. It became a staple of MS-DOS and early Windows games because it handled alpha transparency when almost nothing else did.
Quake, Doom and countless 3D engines shipped textures as TGA. Today it lingers in 3D tools and legacy game assets.
tga.how:
TGA supports uncompressed and RLE-compressed pixels, indexed or true-color, with an optional alpha channel. Its header is tiny and the format is easy to stream.

pcx.tagline: The DOS paint format that time forgot.

meta.title: PCX — history, ZSoft, RLE compression, DOS era
meta.description: PCX explained: ZSoft's 1980s Paintbrush format, early RLE compression, where it survives — and PCX → PNG/JPEG conversion.

pcx.history:
PCX was created by ZSoft in 1985 for PC Paintbrush, one of the first popular DOS painting programs. It rode the early PC graphics wave and was everywhere in the late-80s shareware scene.
As Windows and true-color formats arrived, PCX faded. You mainly find it in old archives and retro software now.
pcx.how:
PCX uses simple run-length encoding (RLE): repeat-byte counts compress solid areas without complex math. It supports 1–32 bit color and a palette.
The format is obsolete but trivial to decode. UWC converts PCX → PNG/JPEG server-side for those occasional legacy files.

meta.title: XBM — history, X Bitmaps, C source images
meta.description: XBM explained: the X Window System bitmap, images as C source code, why it is obsolete — and XBM → PNG/JPEG conversion.

xbm.history:
XBM (X BitMap) came from the X Window System in the late 1980s. Its bizarre feature: an XBM image is valid C source — an array of bytes you #include, and the compiler "draws" it.
That made icons trivially embeddable in X11 programs. Browsers dropped XBM support years ago, but the format lives in retro and security-curiosity circles.
xbm.how:
An XBM is plain text: #define width 16, #define height 16, then static unsigned char bits[] = ﹛ 0x00, 0xFF, ... ﹜. Each bit is one pixel (1 = black).
Reading it is reading C. UWC converts XBM → PNG/JPEG on the server, since no browser will touch it anymore.

meta.description: AIFF explained: Apple's Audio Interchange File Format, uncompressed PCM, why studios love it — and AIFF conversion in the studio.

aiff.history:
AIFF (Audio Interchange File Format) was developed by Apple in 1988, based on the IFF container from Electronic Arts. It was Apple's answer to the sampling workstations of the era.
Because it stores raw PCM with no compression, AIFF became a favorite in pro audio and mastering, where every lost bit matters. Think of it as WAV's Apple cousin.
aiff.how:
AIFF wraps uncompressed PCM samples in IFF "chunks": COMM holds format info, SSND holds the raw audio. No quality loss, but large files — a 3-minute track is ~30 MB.

caf.title: CAF

meta.title: CAF — history, Core Audio Format, 64-bit chunks
meta.description: CAF explained: Apple's Core Audio Format, why it replaced AIFF, 64-bit safe — and CAF conversion in the studio.

caf.history:
CAF (Core Audio Format) was introduced by Apple in 2005 with Mac OS X 10.4 to fix AIFF's limits: AIFF capped files at 4 GB (32-bit sizes) and choked on metadata.
CAF uses 64-bit chunk sizes and a flexible tag system, so it handles huge recordings and rich annotations. It is the native format of Logic Pro.
caf.how:
Like AIFF, CAF is a chunk container, but every field is 64-bit and chunks can nest. It can hold PCM, AAC, or any codec Apple supports, plus markers and regions.

meta.title: Opus — history, IETF RFC 6716, hybrid codec
meta.description: Opus explained: the IETF's royalty-free codec, SILK + CELT, why it wins for voice and music — and Opus conversion in the studio.

opus.history:
Opus was standardized by the IETF as RFC 6716 in 2012, merging Skype's SILK (speech) and Xiph's CELT (music) codecs. The result is a single codec that excels at both conversation and concert.
It is the default for Discord, WhatsApp, and WebRTC — anywhere real-time voice matters. At 32 kbps it sounds better than MP3 at 128.
opus.how:
Opus switches internally between a speech model (good below 20 ms frames) and a music model, even within one stream. It scales from 6 kbps to 510 kbps with very low latency.

meta.title: M4A — history, AAC in an MP4 container, iTunes
meta.description: M4A explained: AAC audio in the MP4 container, why Apple pushed it over MP3, where it lives — and M4A conversion in the studio.

m4a.history:
M4A is not a codec but a container: the MP4 box holding AAC (or ALAC) audio, popularized by Apple's iTunes in the mid-2000s. The ".m4a" extension was Apple's way to mark "audio only, no video."
AAC inside delivers better quality than MP3 at the same bitrate, which is why M4A became the default for purchased and ripped music on Apple devices.

Structurally M4A is an ISO Base Media file (like MP4) whose tracks are audio atoms (moov, mdat). The codec is usually AAC, sometimes ALAC for lossless.

meta.description: WebM audio explained: Google's open container, Vorbis and Opus inside, why it competes with MP4 — and WebM conversion in the studio.

meta.title: QOA — history, the Quite OK Audio format, minimal decoder
meta.description: QOA explained: the Quite OK Audio format, a deliberately tiny lossy codec, ~200-line decoder — and QOA conversion in the studio.

QOA (Quite OK Audio) was published in 2023 by Dominic Szablewski as a reaction to codec bloat: a lossy format whose entire decoder fits in ~200 lines of C. No patents, no committees.

meta.title: ROT47 — history, the 94-character shift, ASCII obfuscation
meta.description: ROT47 explained: the ROT13 variant that also scrambles digits and symbols, the 33–126 range — and an instant ROT47 converter.

rot47.history:
ROT47 is a twist on ROT13 from the Usenet/IRC era: instead of shifting only the 26 letters, it shifts all 94 printable ASCII characters (codes 33–126). The joke is the same — obfuscation, not security.
It became a quick "make this unreadable at a glance" trick for source snippets and chat, since numbers and punctuation get scrambled too.
rot47.how:
Each character in the 33–126 range moves 47 positions forward, wrapping around that 94-character window. So letters, digits and symbols all rotate together.
Like ROT13 it is self-inverse: apply it twice and you are back. UWC applies ROT47 to any printable ASCII in your browser, instantly.

caesar.title: Caesar cipher
caesar.tagline: The cipher that started them all.

meta.title: Caesar cipher — history, Julius Caesar, shift by three
meta.description: Caesar cipher explained: the oldest known encryption, shift by 3, why it is trivial to break — and an instant Caesar converter.

caesar.history:
The Caesar cipher is attributed to Julius Caesar, who (per Suetonius) shifted letters by three to keep military messages private. It is arguably the first documented encryption in the West.
It survived two millennia as a teaching example of substitution ciphers — and as a children's puzzle. Nobody has considered it secure since roughly the fall of Rome.
caesar.how:
Each letter moves a fixed number of places down the alphabet: with shift 3, A→D, B→E. Non-letters pass through. UWC lets you pick any shift, not just 3.
It is broken by trying all 25 shifts (brute force is instant) or by frequency analysis. Fun, historical, and cryptographically useless — exactly as intended here.

meta.title: Atbash — history, Hebrew origins, the alphabet reversed
meta.description: Atbash explained: the ancient Hebrew substitution cipher, alphabet reversed, where it appears in the Bible — and an instant Atbash converter.

atbash.history:
Atbash is one of the oldest ciphers, used with the Hebrew alphabet in the Book of Jeremiah and the Dead Sea Scrolls. "Atbash" comes from the first and last Hebrew letters, aleph and tav.
It later appeared in medieval European mysticism and puzzles. Like Caesar, it is a monoalphabetic substitution — elegant, ancient, and trivially breakable.
atbash.how:
You reverse the alphabet: A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X. The first letter maps to the last, the second to the second-last. It works for Latin and Cyrillic alike.
Because the rule is fixed and self-inverse, Atbash offers zero secrecy — but it is a neat historical curiosity. UWC applies it to Latin and Cyrillic in your browser.

meta.title: Morse code — history, Samuel Morse, telegraph alphabet
meta.description: Morse code explained: the telegraph alphabet, Samuel Morse and Vail, SOS, why it endures — and instant Morse encode/decode.

morse.history:
Morse code was developed in the 1830s–40s by Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail for the electric telegraph. Letters became dots and dashes whose lengths matched frequency — E is just ".", Q is "−−•−".
It carried the first long-distance messages and saved lives (SOS, •••———•••). Though no longer official for maritime use, radio hams and aviators still learn it.
morse.how:
Each character maps to a pattern of short (dot) and long (dash) signals, separated by gaps. A slash separates words. Both Latin and Cyrillic have standard tables.
UWC encodes text to Morse and decodes it back in your browser — a fun bridge between the telegraph age and today.

a1z26.tagline: A is 1, B is 2, Z is 26.

meta.title: A1Z26 — history, the alphabet-number cipher, puzzle use
meta.description: A1Z26 explained: the simple letter-to-number substitution, why it appears in puzzles and ARGs — and an instant A1Z26 converter.

a1z26.history:
A1Z26 is the most naive cipher imaginable: replace each letter with its position in the alphabet. Its origins are unclear because it is "obvious," but it thrives in puzzles, escape rooms and alternate-reality games.
It is never used for secrecy — a space separated by slashes is the only convention. Its charm is being solvable by a glance.
a1z26.how:
A→1, B→2, … Z→26; a slash or space separates words. That is the entire system. Because there is no key, it offers no security at all.
UWC encodes and decodes A1Z26 in your browser — handy when a puzzle hands you "8 5 12 12 15" and you want "HELLO".

bacon.title: Bacon cipher
bacon.tagline: Hiding words in a’s and b’s.

meta.title: Bacon cipher — history, Francis Bacon, binary steganography
meta.description: Bacon cipher explained: Francis Bacon's 1605 binary cipher, 5-bit letters, steganography — and an instant Bacon converter.

bacon.history:
The Bacon cipher was described by Sir Francis Bacon in 1605 — centuries before binary computing. He encoded letters as 5-bit sequences of two symbols (then "a"/"b", now 0/1), and suggested hiding them in innocent text via font styles.
It is the conceptual ancestor of steganography and binary encoding: meaning rides on a difference the eye is trained to ignore.
bacon.how:
Each letter becomes five symbols from a two-symbol alphabet (e.g. A=aaaaa, B=aaaab). You can then disguise the string inside another message — say, by varying letter case or typeface.
UWC encodes text to Bacon and decodes it back in your browser, working with the classic a/b mapping.

tap.title: Tap code

meta.title: Tap code — history, POW communication, Polybius square
meta.description: Tap code explained: the grid knock cipher, Vietnam POWs, the 5×5 Polybius square — and an instant Tap code converter.

tap.history:
Tap code is a knock-based cipher built on the Polybius square: a 5×5 grid of letters addressed by row and column. It became famous among American POWs in Vietnam, who tapped messages through prison walls.
Because you only need to count taps, it works without sight or sound equipment — a lifeline of communication under isolation.
tap.how:
Each letter is two numbers (row, column) in a 5×5 grid (I and J share a cell). You tap the row count, pause, then the column count. "E" (row1,col1) is one tap, a pause, one tap.
UWC encodes and decodes Tap code in your browser — a quiet nod to one of history's most human ciphers.

baudot.title: Baudot / ITA2
baudot.tagline: The 5-bit code that wired the telegraph.

meta.title: Baudot code — history, Émile Baudot, the 5-bit telegraph alphabet
meta.description: Baudot explained: the 1870s 5-bit telegraph code, ITA2, shift characters, why "baud" is named for it — and an instant Baudot converter.

baudot.history:
Baudot code was invented by Émile Baudot in 1870 for multiplexed telegraphy — sending several messages at once. It was the first practical character code and the namesake of "baud" (symbols per second).
Standardized as ITA2, it ran teletypes (TTYs) well into the 20th century. Its 5 bits meant only 32 codes — so it needed shift characters for letters vs figures.
baudot.how:
Each character is 5 bits, but 32 combinations are too few for letters + digits + punctuation. ITA2 solves this with Figures (006) and Letters (007) shift codes that flip the meaning of later symbols.
UWC encodes and decodes Baudot/ITA2 in your browser — a working relic of the telegraph age.
