ebcdic.title: EBCDIC

meta.title: EBCDIC — history, IBM's 1960s mainframe encoding, 8-bit
meta.description: EBCDIC explained: IBM's 8-bit character set, why it differs from ASCII, its mainframe legacy — and an instant EBCDIC converter.

ebcdic.history:
EBCDIC (Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code) was designed by IBM in 1963 for its System/360 mainframes. It evolved from punched-card codes and predates ASCII's final form.
IBM bet on it; the rest of the world bet on ASCII. Decades later, EBCDIC still runs on mainframes in banks and insurers — a legacy that refuses to die.
ebcdic.how:
Like ASCII it is 8-bit, but the code points are arranged completely differently: 'A' is 0xC1 in EBCDIC but 0x41 in ASCII. Control characters sit in odd places.
Moving text between a mainframe and the web means translating the two. UWC converts EBCDIC ↔ ASCII in your browser for those legacy integrations.

fullwidth.title: Full-width / Half-width

meta.title: Full-width forms — history, CJK typography, Unicode compatibility
meta.description: Full-width/half-width explained: why CJK text needs square Latin chars, Unicode compatibility ranges — and an instant full↔half converter.

fullwidth.history:
In Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK) typography, every character occupies a square "full-width" cell. Mixing in Latin text looked ragged, so Unicode added full-width versions of A–Z, 0–9 and punctuation — each as wide as a CJK glyph.
There are also half-width katakana for the reverse direction. These ranges exist mainly for compatibility with legacy encodings like Shift-JIS.
fullwidth.how:
Full-width A (U+FF21) is the visual twin of ASCII A (U+0041) but twice as wide. Converting is a fixed code-point offset within the compatibility blocks.
UWC switches text between full-width and half-width forms in your browser — useful for normalizing CJK documents or fixing copy-paste artifacts.

zalgo.title: Zalgo
zalgo.tagline: The text that appears to glitch.

meta.title: Zalgo text — history, combining marks, creepypasta
meta.description: Zalgo explained: stacking Unicode combining marks, the "corrupted" look, its creepypasta origin — and an instant Zalgo encoder/remover.

zalgo.history:
Zalgo text is the Internet's "corrupted" aesthetic: characters draped in cascading diacritics, as if possessed. The name comes from "Zalgo," a creepypasta meme of an eldritch force that breaks reality.
Technically it is just Unicode combining marks piled on a base letter. The effect is pure styling — no data is actually lost.
zalgo.how:
Unicode lets you attach many combining marks (U+0300–U+036F) to one character; stacking dozens makes glyphs smear upward and downward. Rendering depends on the font.
UWC adds Zalgo for fun and strips it back to clean text — the marks are just zero-width decorations. All in your browser.

leet.title: Leet speak

meta.title: Leet speak — history, 1980s hacker slang, letter substitution
meta.description: Leet explained: "1337" subculture, substituting letters with numbers/symbols, its BBS origins — and an instant leet converter.

leet.history:
Leet (from "elite") emerged in 1980s bulletin-board systems (BBS) as insider slang. Users swapped letters for look-alike digits and symbols: E→3, A→4, T→7, S→5. It signaled belonging to the "leet" crowd.
It later leaked into gaming tags, memes, and "pr0n"-style spelling. Pure subculture — a cipher only in the loosest sense.
leet.how:
There is no single rule; common swaps are A→4, E→3, I→1, O→0, S→5, T→7, and stylized variants like "0wn3d". Intensity ranges from mild to unreadable.
UWC applies a standard leet mapping to your text in the browser — flip it on for flavor, flip it off to recover the words.

meta.title: Slugify — history, URL slugs, SEO-friendly links
meta.description: Slugify explained: converting titles to URL-safe strings, lowercasing, dashes, transliteration — and an instant slugify tool.

slugify.history:
A "slug" is the human-readable part of a URL: /blog/what-is-a-slug. The term came from newsprint ("slug" = a short headline). Web platforms generate slugs so links are readable, indexable, and shareable.
Every CMS — WordPress, Django, Ghost — slugifies post titles automatically. It is invisible plumbing that makes the web friendlier.
slugify.how:
Slugifying lowercases text, replaces spaces with hyphens, strips punctuation, and often transliterates accents (café → cafe). The result is safe in a URL with no encoding.

translit.title: Translit

meta.title: Translit — history, Russian Latin transliteration, GOST vs ISO
meta.description: Translit explained: mapping Cyrillic to Latin, the GOST/ISO systems, why Russians type "privet" — and an instant translit converter.

translit.history:
Translit maps Cyrillic letters to Latin ones, born from necessity: early Russian keyboards and SMS only had Latin keys, so people spelled Russian with Latin letters (привет → privet).
Formal systems exist too — GOST and ISO transliteration — for passports and library catalogs. The casual version is just what feels right to a typist.
translit.how:
There is no single table: "ч" might be "ch" or "4", "ш" might be "sh" or "6". UWC uses a common Russian↔Latin mapping so you can convert both ways in the browser.
Handy for recovering text typed in translit, or generating a Latin spelling from Cyrillic without a dictionary.
